articles.title: Rugby Union: Eddie Hearn expected to up Prem influence
articles.summary: Renowned boxing promoter Eddie Hearn is expected to ramp up his influence in rugby union after meeting with Prem bosses in Monaco last week.
articles.body:
Renowned boxing promoter Eddie Hearn is expected to ramp up his influence in rugby union after meeting with Prem bosses in Monaco last week.

Hearn, who runs Matchroom Sport, has made a foray into rugby by signing high-profile players Finn Russell and Henry Pollock to his stable.

And the sports mogul has been backed to make a big impact in the sport by senior figures in the English game.

"[Matchroom] will be a force for good. [Hearn] sees that rugby is on a great trajectory and he's very pro the Prem," said Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor.

"I think his ambition goes beyond just representing top athletes.

"He doesn't want to be a disruptor. He wants to work with the league, but he definitely wants to agitate for more growth and sees a lot of potential."

Hearn has spoken previously of his desire to "turbo-charge" the profile of rugby union and its players, adding it would be a "stroll in the park" to transform the sport.

"I'd expect him to represent some more of the top stars in the Prem," said Massie-Taylor.

"And so you start to move into other options, whether that's around events, big games, or something specifically commercial around the players across the league.

"I don't think he's there to buy a rugby club, but he could definitely help introduce people to it and partner with that."

Massie-Taylor was speaking around the release of the Prem's second annual financial monitoring report, which revealed that all 10 clubs have passed the financial standards for the 2026/2027 season.

Following the demise of London Irish, Wasps and Worcester, the Prem has tightened up its rules with clubs now required to be more transparent over the state of their finances.

According to the report the financial picture has improved across the league, with revenues up and club losses forecast to reduce by £26.7m, while Newcastle Red Bulls, Exeter Chiefs and Bath Rugby have all secured major external investment over the past 12 months.

However no club is yet in profit, with Saracens and Sale reporting the heaviest losses.

"In the next five years we would expect the vast majority of clubs to move into the black," said Massie-Taylor.

"And for those that don't the losses would be relatively marginal. But I think there will be a situation when clubs move into a more sustainable position, there will be a desire to re-invest.

"So as long as the asset is growing quicker than the aggregate losses, then you have value."

'We are looking to develop English clubs'

The report reiterates the plan for the Prem to increase from 10 to 12 teams by the 2030/31 season, with expression of interests to be completed in the coming months.

Massie-Taylor confirmed future entrants to the Prem must play at least one season in the second-tier Champ and would also need a large cash advance to purchase a "P-Share", which is thought to be valued at around £20m.

It's understood the Welsh Rugby Union has approached the Prem about the possibility of Welsh sides joining to form an Anglo-Welsh league, and while not shutting the door completely on the prospect, Massie-Taylor said the priority remains to develop clubs in the English system.

"The assumption when we were doing Project Forge [English rugby's strategic plan] was that we were looking to develop English clubs," he added.

"That's where we see a lot of potential, whether that's clubs within the Champ, clubs that maybe are outside the Champ and in the English system elsewhere, and previous clubs [for example a reborn Wasps or London Irish].

"So we're putting a lot of resource and attention in developing them. It wasn't a debate at the time around Welsh clubs."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England lose 24-6 to Samoa and make group-stage exit from women's tournament
articles.summary: Freedom Crichton Ropati scored a hat-trick as Samoa claimed a 24-6 win over England in Wollongong; England fail to qualify for the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals after two defeats in their three pool matches
articles.body:
Stuart Barrow's side needed victory to secure a top-two finish in Group A and qualify for a third consecutive World Cup semi-final, only to see their campaign ended by a second successive loss.

Freedom Crichton Ropati scored a first-half hat-trick as Samoa raced into a 12-0 lead at the break, with Mercedez Taulelei-Siala extending the Pacific islanders' advantage early in the second half.

Evie Cousins scored England's only try as they looked to battle back into the contest in captain Jodie Cunningham's final match, but Samoa held firm and extended their winning margin with Pauline Piliae-Rasabale's late score.

England's defeat follows a 15-try thrashing by Australia on Saturday and sees them end the pool stage in third spot on two points, joining Wales - who they beat 70-6 in their tournament opener - in making an early exit.

How Samoa ended England's World Cup hopes

Destin Mino-Sinapati nearly got Samoa off to the dream start but failed to ground the ball cleanly in the corner, only for them to hit the front in the ninth minute when Ropati acrobatically dived over in the corner.

Samoa piled on further pressure and exploited space on offer by England, with a sweeping move seeing Ekepati offload for Ropati to score again on 19 minutes.

England failed to make inroads during the opening 35 minutes, with Roach knocking on less than 20 metres from the line during a rare attack, before Ropati completed her hat-trick in the 29th minute with another score in the right corner.

All three touchline conversions during the first half were missed by Pauline Piliae-Rasabale, who also failed to kick the extras when Taulelei-Siala touched down early in the second half to end an impressive right-to-left move.

Cousins offered England a lifeline in the 41st minute, rolling through Tyra Ekepati's attempted tackle to complete a powerful score, with Isabel Rowe adding the extras to leave them within 10 points of their opponents.

Samoa were gifted a penalty under the posts a few minutes later after a ball strip from Lucie Sams, with Piliae-Rasabale taking the two-pointer, although England remained in the contest heading into the closing stages.

England wasted a chance to make it a one-try game when Fran Goldthorp threw a forward overhead pass to Anna Davies, who would have been free to score, with qualification hopes ended when Rimoni went over in the 66th minute.

Rimoni's try under the posts - converted by Piliae-Rasabale - sparked wild celebrations from Samoa, who are through to the semi-finals for the first time in their history.

Samoa progress as England 'sad to be going home'

"I think we lost to the better side on the day, I'm not going to deny that. I thought it was a good game and it's a good game for England to be in, because we have a problem at the moment.

"We play France or Wales and - no disrespect to those nations - but we win them, and then we play Jillaroos and we lose heavily, so this was quite a nice game to be in where it was competitive all the way. The more of those we could get as a nation would definitely help us.

"We had a very young group, average age of 21 and a half, 22 across the group. A lot of those players will go on in four years time and be better for this experience and that's a good place to leave it, but we're very sad to be going home."

"This group of girls is really special. It's been an honour to captain the side and play in four World Cups. I've lived my dream a million times over. The girls gave everything out there today and it didn't stick.

"Samoa were fantastic and I wish them all the best in the next round."

Samoa qualify for the semi-finals and will face the winners of Group A - likely New Zealand - on November 7 in Newcastle.

The other semi-final sees Australia face the runners-up of Group B the following day, before the final is held in Brisbane on November 15.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Spirited England exit World Cup after Samoa loss
articles.summary: England exit the Women's Rugby League World Cup as Samoa beat them 24-6 in their Group A decider in Wollongong.
articles.body:
Tries: Crichton Ropati 3, Taulelei-Siala, Fanua Rimoni

Goal: Piliae-Rasabale Penalty: Piliae-Rasabale

England's women took one step back in the hope of taking two forward as they exited the Rugby League World Cup at the group stage.

With Stuart Barrow's side defeated by Samoa - despite a spirited display - their focus immediately shifts forward to 2030.

Whether that long-term strategy will bear dividends, though, is as uncertain as the location of the tournament in four years' time, which is yet to be confirmed.

After reaching the semi-final stage at the previous four World Cups, England's eye was clearly on the future this time.

That was reflected in Barrow's thinking for this tournament when he named a squad containing 11 players aged 23 or under.

While the 70-6 rout of a Wales team ill-equipped to compete at this level on their bow had been anticipated and briefly raised expectation levels, what has followed has only underlined the gulf in class England still have to bridge.

And having been humbled again by the Jillaroos just under a week ago, any suggestions that the experience was the "best preparation" they could have for a make-or-break final group game were trashed on Friday in Wollongong.

Instead, the great power and pace of the Samoa players showed almost straight away.

Freedom Crichton Ropati twice went over in the right corner as England fought a rearguard action and the Parramatta Eels winger completed her hat-trick before the break as Samoa enjoyed a huge territorial advantage.

And it looked ominous for England when Mercedez Taulelei-Siala capitalised on a huge overload down the left to score straight after half-time and extend Samoa's lead to 16-0.

However, when Evie Cousins, who had been in tears towards the end of the first period after failing to catch a routine high ball, skipped over in the left corner, after a superb line break from Hollie-Mae Dodd, it sparked England back into life.

Isabel Rowe added the extras and when Pauline Piliae-Rasabale elected to take two points from a penalty for Samoa it underlined the pressure that Barrow's side had been able to apply.

While England went out in the last four on a dark and dank night in York four years ago, their departure from this World Cup was in an altogether more scenic setting, with the Pacific Ocean as the backdrop.

Had Fran Goldthorp been able to offload without her pass straying forward, when England had two players spare and the try-line at their mercy, it could have made for an entirely different conclusion.

Instead, when they then failed to find touch after winning a penalty, they were punished ruthlessly as Fanua Rimoni crashed over for Samoa's fifth try to seal their passage into the last four and a meeting with New Zealand.

England edge towards World Cup exit despite PNG win

England thrash Wales to begin World Cup defence

England out of Women's RL World Cup as Samoa reach semi-finals

It was certainly not the ending that Jodie Cunningham wanted or perhaps deserved.

For so long a trailblazer of the women's game in England, this tournament represented the swansong of a distinguished playing career after 38 caps and four World Cups.

However, the 34-year-old will take heart from the rays of hope in this England performance.

The big question now is if that can translate into making them genuine contenders in 2030, or whether they will be still hamstrung as part-time players in a game that is making rapid professional advancements in the southern hemisphere.

articles.title: Wales aim to cap 2026 revival with WXV Global Series double over Japan
articles.summary: Wales have the opportunity to finish the international year on a high on Saturday as they seek to complete a WXV double over Japan.
articles.body:
Wales have the opportunity to finish the international year on a high on Saturday as they seek to complete the double over Japan.

Sean Lynn's side have already racked up two wins from three in the WXV Global Series, including last weekend's 17-0 victory in Tokyo.

And while they go into the contest as favourites, Lynn insists they will not be taking the Sakura Fifteen lightly, especially given recent performances against Ireland.

"We were wary about them last Saturday and we see no difference this week," he said.

"Japan are very efficient, very regimented. Some of their defensive displays were very good [last weekend] and they're a hard side to break down."

Victory would not see Wales break back into the world's top 10, but will certainly be progress for a side which previously went nine Test matches without a win.

The question is, can they cap 2026's revival with one last W?

Kumagaya Rugby Stadium, Saitama Prefecture

Live on iplayer and BBC Sport website & app. Audio commentary on Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra & BBC Radio Cymru.

Why winning ugly is just as important for Wales

Wales grind out frustrating WXV win against Japan

The fact that Lynn has boldly made five starting changes shows the strength in depth he has built in the squad during his 18 months in charge.

Bethan Lewis, Gwenllian Pyrs, Lleucu George, Gwen Crabb and Courtney Keight - who have a combined 248 Test caps - are all back in the XV having impressed off the bench last weekend.

"Certain individuals went really well, they deserve those starts," said Lynn.

"Gwenllian Pyrs, the way she tightened up that scrum in the second half was really pleasing for us. Gwen Crabb and Bethan Lewis are very good set piece operators.

"And then Lleucu George, some of her territorial game was good, but also her passing game was exciting."

Keight comes in for the injured Freya Bell, one of the youngsters to have impressed since stepping up to senior level earlier this year.

Co-captain Alex Callender moves to number eight as the one positional switch.

Japan have made three starting changes, with Komachi Imakugi getting the nod at full-back and Mele Yua Havili Kagawa coming onto the wing.

Flanker Nduka Jennier is the only change to the pack.

Number eight Savannah Bodman and centre Sophie Akiko Langford retain their places after impressing on debut last week, while scrum-half Moe Tsukui will lead the side out at Kumagaya Rugby Stadium.

Hosts Japan have not tasted victory since beating Hong King China to secure their seventh consecutive Asia Rugby Women's Championship in May.

But there have been some notable performances, including pushing Ireland all the way in Galway in the first of last month's double-header.

Wales are looking to back-up last weekend's performance, which was the first time they had kept a clean sheet in eight years.

Victory on Saturday would also see Wales secure back-to-back Test wins for the first time since June 2024.

Quiz: Name the 12 players given Wales debuts by Lynn

Bell ruled out of Wales' second WXV Japan Test

Wales co-captain Alex Callender said there was a frustration in camp after last weekend, but nilling a team away from home was "a pretty good scoreline".

"We know that Japan will be wounded and that they'll be coming out for 80 minutes again," she said.

"It's about backing up the win but also putting in a better performance to come off the field and really know that we've given everything.

"Hopefully we can play a little bit more free-flowing rugby and enjoy it a lot more."

Reflecting on the campaign as a whole, Callender added: "We spoke about what we wanted to get out of this WXV, and if we can come away with a result this weekend, I'd be so proud of the girls."

BBC Wales commentator Gareth Rhys Owen said: "Wales won ugly last weekend. The 17-0 victory was a pretty horrible game to watch, but they found a way to win in difficult conditions.

"Perhaps the most encouraging sign of progress was how self-critical Wales were afterwards. For so long, the conversation has been about finding positives in defeat. Now they're identifying shortcomings in victory. That's a significant shift in mentality.

"The selection of Lleucu George ahead of Keira Bevan at fly-half is also intriguing. Wales will eventually have to settle on their first-choice number 10 and build some continuity.

"Before this double-header, Wales would surely have taken two ugly wins over Japan. They probably still would."

Little Angel makes big impact on return to Japan

Wales make five changes as Lynn rewards bench

Japan: Imakugi; Tsunokawa, Langford, Kataoka, Havili Kagawa; Harada, Tsukui; Komaki, Nagaoka, Kitano, Kawamura, Sato, Asari, Jennifer, Bodman

Replacements: Kuge, Mine, Fuji, M Nishimura, Korai, Seo, Ito, S Nishimura

Wales: Neumann; N Metcalfe, Cox, Keight, A Williams; George, Lockwood, Pyrs, K Jones, Tuipulotu, B Metcalfe, Crabb, K Williams (co-capt), Lewis, Callender (co-capt).

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England edge towards exit despite PNG win
articles.summary: England's points chase against Papua New Guinea descends into an error-strewn 34-12 win that will almost certainly lead to their World Cup exit.
articles.body:
Tries: Ashton, Brimson, Young, Smith, Knowles, Lewis

England edged towards a World Cup exit after their points chase against Papua New Guinea descended into a chaotic and error-strewn victory that will almost certainly prove insufficient in the final reckoning.

Since their opening loss to Tonga, England's objective had been simple in their two remaining group games. Win and win well to have any hope of the reaching the last four.

They achieved that objective against France with a crushing 82-0 triumph and looked on course to make significant inroads into the 68-point deficit they needed to make up on Samoa when they led 22-0 after 22 minutes, courtesy of tries from Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Dominic Young and Harry Smith.

However, things went badly wrong from there on despite head coach Brian McDermott urging his players to be patient in the build-up to this fixture.

A combination of repeatedly coughing up possession and conceding penalties restored belief in the Papua New Guinea ranks and Dudley Dotoi and Gairo Voro cashed in with tries for the Kumuls as England threw away the initiative.

The sight of England centre Herbie Farnworth being stripped of the ball running towards the try line moments before Mikey Lewis added another try to Morgan Knowles' second-half effort aptly summed up how things had slipped away.

England were guilty of making 21 errors and delivered a performance that included just a 57% completion rate, hardly good enough at this - or any - level.

It was the total opposite of the blueprint from the France game and it means England can now only reach the last four if Tonga defeat Samoa by more than 46 points.

As good as Kristian Woolf's side are, that appears highly improbable given they lost 34-6 to Samoa 12 months ago in Brisbane and have not registered a win over their neighbours since 2018.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Wales make two changes to face Australia
articles.summary: After back-to-back heavy defeats to England and Samoa, Wales end their debut campaign against champions Australia.
articles.body:
Head coach Tom Brindle has made two personnel changes to his squad for Wales' final 2026 Rugby League World Cup fixture against reigning champions Australia on Sunday, 1 November (04:40 GMT)

Wales, playing at their first World Cup, have lost both of their opening Pool A games, falling 70-6 against England and 76-0 against Samoa .

Dual-code international Ffion Lewis replaces Amberley Ruck at stand-off, with Carys Marsh moving from the interchange bench to starting hooker.

Lucia Davies could make her first appearance of the tournament from the bench, while Dani McGifford returns as the 18th player after missing out last week.

Hooker Jasmine Gibbons has been forced to miss out against top-ranked Australia after failing a head injury assessment late on in the defeat by Samoa.

While Wales have conceded 146 points across their opening two fixtures, Australia, who are bidding for a fourth straight World Cup title, have conceded none.

They kept England and Samoa at bay, both of whom scored at least 13 tries against Wales, while scoring 118 points of their own.

The Jillaroos have lost one international since 2016, while Wales only played their first official international in 2021, with this being only their 16th fixture.

articles.title: Kepu Tuipulotu a doubt for England's Nations Championship campaign with knee injury
articles.summary: Uncapped hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has suffered a knee injury in training and will not be included in England's squad for the Australia fixture on 8 November.
articles.body:
Hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has emerged as a doubt for England's Nations Championship campaign after picking up a knee injury in national training on Tuesday.

The uncapped 21-year-old had been tipped to make his England breakthrough this autumn.

However, it is understood he will not be included in the England squad for the opener with Australia on 8 November, with an exact timeframe on his return unclear.

Tuipulotu also qualifies for Wales, the country of his birth, and was even invited to train with the senior side by then-coach Warren Gatland but opted to focus on England.

He joined Bath's academy in 2024 and signed a contract with the club until 2028 earlier this year.

Scrum-half Archie McParland is also an injury concern, and has not been included in the Northampton squad to face Gloucester at the weekend, while fly-half Fin Smith is a major doubt for the Wallabies fixture.

In more positive injury news, Gloucester Seb Atkinson has been named at inside centre for the Cherry and Whites as he bids to prove his fitness.

England also face Japan and New Zealand next month, before the Nations Championship finals weekend at the end of November.

articles.title: WXV Global Series: Ireland 'have it in us' to claim Springboks series win
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says his side are ready for their "second ascent" as they target a historic series win over South Africa.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Scott Bemand said his side are ready for their "second ascent" as they target a historic series win over South Africa.

No Irish side has ever won back-to-back Test matches on Springbok soil, but, following last weekend's 40-27 win , Bemand's team have the chance to make history when they take on the same opponents in Cape Town on Saturday (13:00 GMT).

Bemand is hopeful his side can end the WXV Series and the year on a high by backing up last week's impressive first victory.

"We were delighted last week. That was a really important game, if you're going to play a series, getting the first win on the board is a massive event," Bemand said.

"That leads us to this week, the second ascent and a second chance to back up the win. To get a series win over South Africa would be historic.

"It's important for us to finish with another winning performance. We've got it in us, it's a massive challenge with the physicality and the South African environment, but for us to finish the year on a winning note would be a big point for us."

Ireland make two changes for second Springboks Test

'It's going to take an even bigger effort this week'

Bemand has made two changes for the second game at Athlone Stadium.

Niamh Gallagher replaces Stacey Flood at full-back while Aoibheann Reilly is recalled at scrum-half as Emily Lane drops to the bench.

"Aoibheann and Emily have been going toe-to-toe. I thought Emily had a great game last week and she had a run for us in the Six Nations. It's a bit of rotation and giving Aoibheann a shot from the start," Bemand explained.

"Niamh has been going really well in training and we have been really impressed with how she went in that second Japanese game and she's earned the right to come have a crack at it."

Bemand was pleased with how Ireland coped with South Africa's physicality in the first Test, particularly in a thrilling opening 40 minutes, but warned they will have to go to another level to topple the Springboks once more.

"We knew it would be a really tough start, they're always there or thereabouts at half-time so we knew they'd be a massive physical challenge to start with and our players did everything they needed to and wanted to do to put ourselves in a position to get the game flowing in the second half," he added.

"We know it's going to take an even bigger effort this week, that we'll have to overcome the physicality again but from what I've seen in training, we will make sure we get the scoreboard ticking away form South Africa at the end of the game."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong
articles.summary: England's men and women endured different types of disappointment at the Rugby League World Cup on Friday - and the inquests have already begun.
articles.body:
As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were already being written for England's Men's Rugby League World Cup campaign.

Much earlier on Friday, England's women had lacked the power and nous to overcome Samoa, losing 24-6 in a match that decided who went through to the semi-finals.

England's men actually won their game - 34-12 - but it was nowhere near the margin of victory required. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.

And so the likelihood is that for the first time in World Cup history, neither England's men nor their women will feature in the last four.

For the men, that ends a run that began with Great Britain at the first tournament in 1954.

The disappointment will only reinforce the idea that English rugby league needs a serious period of introspection - as well as significant investment to keep pace with the game in the southern hemisphere.

But there have been other factors to trouble England at this World Cup, hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea at short notice after France pulled out for financial reasons.

Even before a ball was kicked, the men were faced with a sense of impending doom - brought on by injuries, shambolic travel arrangements and a bizarre format that had England facing immediate jeopardy with a testing opener against Tonga.

England edge towards World Cup exit despite PNG win

Spirited England out of World Cup after Samoa loss

The northern hemisphere game has deep-rooted problems, and seems to be stuck in stasis when compared with the thriving NRL.

England had a record of being a major player at World Cups - having reached two finals and a further four semi-finals at the past six tournaments.

But when last autumn's 3-0 Ashes series defeat by Australia prompted the departure of head coach Shaun Wane, his successor was handed a near-impossible task.

Brian McDermott was appointed in April. Given just six months to prepare, the former Leeds Rhinos head coach had no mid-season international to work on a plan. Based in Australia because of his role as Gold Coast Titans assistant coach, he relied on virtual meetings to connect with his prospective squad and staff.

Four on-field sessions were planned in Australia before the World Cup. But only two were completed in full after his UK-based players were subjected to a 48-hour journey to Perth that left them exhausted - a situation McDermott compared to Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the 1987 road-trip comedy starring Steve Martin and John Candy.

It was a shambolic way to prepare for a pivotal opener against Tonga - one that always had the potential to consign the defeated team to an early elimination.

Following that 30-12 loss, McDermott said: "You give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament and I'd be really excited."

With the tournament organisers planning travel itineraries for the teams involved, any post-World Cup debrief ought to examine how that situation was allowed to occur.

It would have made more sense for England's opener to be against France - the only other team in the men's tournament made up largely of northern hemisphere-based players.

Wakefield Trinity's historic triumph may have delivered a wonderful sign-off story to the Super League season but it delivered another conundrum around England's squad selection.

Had McDermott known prior to 5 October that none of the Wakefield players in his thinking would be available, could arrangements have been made for his UK-based players to travel to Australia earlier?

In the end, only three of the 14 England-based players in the squad (George Williams, Matty Ashton and Ben Currie) participated in the Super League Grand Final on 3 October.

"If we come together next year as a group, we will be further down the track and we don't need to start from scratch," McDermott added.

"Bear in mind when we landed in Perth on the Friday [9 October], we are starting... like we didn't know each other.

"We were putting things in place about who we are as a group, what it means to us, how we are going to play, how we are going to attack and how we are going to defend. There's been a ton of work gone on."

While much of the pre-tournament noise centred on the omission of Jake Connor and England's long-running halves debate, very little focus was given to a decimated forward pack and other notable absentees.

Prior the first match, McDermott recounted Australia prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui's admiration for the strength of the English pack during last year's Ashes series.

England's ability to front up had also previously been talked up by Kangaroos boss Kevin Walters.

Yet McDermott had few of those same players at his disposal.

Matty Lees' season-ending injury in May was not only a blow for St Helens but also robbed England of a key enforcer, one who had previously shown he could stand up to the physicality of a powerhouse Tonga front row.

With second-rower Mike McMeeken and prop Caleb Hamlin-Uele unavailable, Morgan Smithies withdrawing from the squad injured and a calf complaint taking Morgan Knowles out of the equation for the encounter against Tonga, England were left short in that area.

That is before you even get to options such as Sydney Roosters' Billy Smith, Wigan's Jake Wardle and Leeds Rhinos duo Ash Handley and Mikolaj Oledzki, all absent through injury.

And when England had to chase the scoreboard after their defeat by Tonga - while hoping results elsewhere went in their favour - it left them in trouble.

They failed to get the numbers on the board they needed against Papua New Guinea. McDermott acknowledged that it left him and his players waiting for the inevitable.

"It feels like we lost the game," he said. "We won and, in any circumstances I would be really proud but I think something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through.

"We've made massive strides together in such a short period of time, in difficult circumstances where the narrative of the last two weeks is that you've got to win by 70 and 60. You don't just need to win, you need to win by massive margins."

Whenever the Women's Rugby League World Cup has featured semi-finals previously, England or Great Britain have always been there. When it has not, they have always finished in the top four.

But this time, they approached the tournament with a different focus, as head coach Staurt Barrow opted for youth over experience.

His squad contained 11 players aged 23 or under, and was largely comprised of players who have full-time occupations away from rugby league.

And that told as England were humbled 78-0 by world champions Australia last Saturday, and found wanting by a Samoa side dominated by NRL Women's Premiership talent. While Australia's domestic league pays its players, money is much tighter in England's Women's Super League.

"Women's Super League has progressed to a certain level and we are bringing young players through so that creeps into the national team," said Barrow.

"It's good and refreshing - but at the same rate we are progressing, it's probably accelerating quicker on this side of the world if I am really honest.

"The investment into the NRLW is not only making the Jillaroos better but it's making all the Pacific nations better as well.

"I think nearly every player for Samoa has played NRLW at some stage and that competition is improving at a rate of knots. We'll have to go back and look at what we can do in our competition.

"We definitely need to do something because the acceleration of the game over here is phenomenal at the moment.

"Back home, we need to have more investment into the women's and girls game. It can't just be a token gesture at some clubs - and I'm not saying it is, but we need to put money into it."

Barrow's other main problem relates to geography and an international calendar that leaves them ill-prepared to face the leading southern hemisphere nations.

Aside from a record 90-4 defeat by Australia in Las Vegas , England's women have been limited to six international fixtures since the previous World Cup, all against France and Wales - in which they have scored 348 points, while conceding four.

"We lost to the better side on the day. I am not going to deny that," Barrow added.

"It was a good game and a good game for England to be in because we have a problem at the moment where we play France or Wales. And no disrespect to those nations but we win them [games] - and we play the Jillaroos and lose heavily.

"This was a nice game to be in where it was competitive all the way. The more of those we can get will definitely help us as a nation."

articles.title: Ellie Kildunne: how Red Roses star ended up benched by England
articles.summary: Ellie Kildunne has been the Red Roses' figurehead throughout their rise to world champions, so why is she on the bench for Friday night's Test against the USA?
articles.body:
She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby World Cup. She's even got her own Barbie doll.

So why isn't Ellie Kildunne starting for England against the USA on Friday night (21:15 kick-off)?

First of all she is human, let's not forget that.

We're all allowed ups and downs. It's just that Kildunne's dip comes with the large spotlight of her being the Red Roses' household name.

None of her team-mates come close to her popularity with fans both in and outside rugby union with her 239,000 Instagram followers. Her face and name are used for clicks by all the media, present company included.

However, if you follow the sport and watch her play, no-one is undroppable.

England suffered their first loss in four years to end their 41-Test unbeaten streak in Toronto against Canada. In that fixture and their previous match with the same opposition in Exeter, Kildunne, 27, was a target for the opposition. She was never given space, defenders stepped up, her arms were pulled and balls were spilt.

When England head coach John Mitchell benched her after England's loss in Toronto he was clear that "it isn't disputed that she adds huge value".

However, he went on to add: "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to help her through that.

"She wants to become consistent as well, and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses.

"So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game, and that goes for everyone."

The key word we can take from that is "consistent" - mainly because Mitchell said it twice.

Kildunne remains one of the world's most phenomenal players when it comes to gainline success and metres gained.

Much of this is due to poor opposition defence, but her statistics show a decline over the past three seasons at international level.

It seems almost harsh to highlight as these are numbers other players could only dream of but she's also gone from beating an average of six defenders a game in 2024, to 4.2 in 2026.

Kildunne has also conceded more penalties in 2026 than either of the previous two years. Some of these statistics, althought not all, are mirrored in her PWR performances last season.

While Canada are not alone, it does appear they are one of the best teams at dealing with Kildunne's threats.

In their drawn match in Exeter, Kildunne made 17 carries for 47 metres, an average of 2.8m, which is well below her usual standards. In Toronto she had the ball turned over twice - that was her joint-most in any England game.

Emma Sing now appears to have some purchase on the England 15 shirt and it is well deserved. She is a different full-back to Kildunne, which is a bonus for the Red Roses.

Sing has three PWR titles with her club side Gloucester-Hartpury and has been one of their most reliable players throughout that period. She has got a monster boot round the park and off the tee and, while Sing might not score the same worldies we have seen from Kildunne, her highlights reel is none too shabby.

On Sing's starting selection in Ottawa, Mitchell was happy to explain the players' differences: "They play quite differently. So we're very fortunate to have two very good full-backs. But you know, Emma's been sitting in the in the wings in this particular phase of our campaign.

"She was intermittent through injury for a long period of time. So she's in a really good physical place, and she's worked really, really hard. So I think it's time to give her an opportunity."

Red Roses make six changes but Kildunne on bench again

How have Canada closed gap to world champions England?

No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning

It is a bit crass, but if you only follow men's rugby, Kildunne is a bit more Marcus Smith, while Sing is a bit more Freddie Steward - they are just different players.

Add to that, Sing was brought up on a Devon sheep farm and is not a huge fan of the media spotlight. That is not to say that Kildunne has coveted it, but she is far more comfortable in the media space.

You also must tip your hat to Kildunne and how she has managed herself with her new-found fame. After England beat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in September, she spent an hour signing autographs and doing selfies to an unrelenting, screaming chorus of "Ellie, Ellie, Ellie".

Managing your own needs as an athlete and the increasing demands of fans is not an easy circle to square.

So where does Kildunne go from here? That is actually the most exciting bit.

No-one with a spiral bomb like she produced in the 2025 Rugby World Cup final is going to fade into the shadows. She is an incredible athlete and rugby player, so the expectation is that, much like Doctor Who, she will just regenerate.

Kildunne 2.0 could end up spending more time on the wing for England initially, but you can only see her fighting for a shirt and getting better.

articles.title: The Prem: Bristol 16-22 Exeter: Leicester dominate Bristol to go top
articles.summary: Leicester take maximum points to go top of the Prem before the rest of the weekend fixtures with a 22-16 win away at Bristol.
articles.body:
Tries: Rees-Zammit Cons: Williams Pens: Williams 3

Tries: Steward, Radwan, Hassell-Collins, Blamire Cons: Searle

Leicester took maximum points to go top of the Prem before the rest of the weekend fixtures with a 22-16 win away at Bristol.

Tries from Freddie Steward and Adam Radwan put Tigers in the driving seat after a sublime score from Louis Rees-Zammit had given Bristol an early lead.

Ollie Hassell-Collins extended Leicester's advantage to 17-7 after the break and while James Williams' two penalties closed the gap, Jamie Blamire drove over for the visitors' fourth to all-but seal victory.

But with Billy Searle missing three conversions, Leicester were not as far clear as they could have been and a third penalty from Williams closed the gap to six points to give Bristol hope in the final minutes.

Yet the hosts had to settle for a single losing bonus point as the Tigers did enough to see out the match and leapfrog Gloucester at the summit, with the Cherry and Whites set to play Northampton on Saturday (17:30 GMT).

Chessum signs new two-year deal with Leicester

Janse van Rensburg set to return in December

Smith out injured as Saints make changes for Gloucester

Both sides came into the game evenly matched with three wins apiece before the autumn international break, and it was the hosts who struck first through a world-class Rees-Zammit try.

The Welsh wing side-stepped his way free and then skipped out of a tackle to run clear and dive under the posts for his fifth Prem try of the season.

Leicester responded, stealing possession to attack on the counter and Searle neatly kicked the ball out wide, where Tigers had numbers, for Steward to score in the corner on his 100th Prem start.

There were chances for more tries at either end as Fitz Harding was held up over the line for Bristol, while the excellent Ollie Chessum got the ball down for Leicester, but it was chalked off for a knock-on beforehand.

Rees-Zammit came inches away from doubling his tally as he shrugged his way out of a tackle and chased down his own chip, only for Tom Whiteley to expertly deny him.

But the momentum shift came just after the half-hour mark when Bristol indiscipline saw them down to 13 thanks to two high tackles in three minutes, with Matias Moroni and Tom Jordan sent to the bin.

With space open everywhere Tigers capitalised and Radwan sprinted sublimely from nowhere to dot down a kick that caught Bristol napping.

After spilling a catch before half-time that would have seen him score, Hassell-Collins got his try the other side of the break, this time easily collecting Searle's crossfield kick in acres of space to stretch the lead to 17-7.

Williams' penalty narrowed the gap and his second eventually brought Bristol within four points with 20 minutes to go.

But Leicester struck again to add the bonus-point score as Blamire walked over at the back of a driving maul.

Still, three missed conversions meant Leicester were not yet home and dry and Williams' third penalty with seven minutes to go set up a tense finale, but Leicester held firm to end the first block of Prem games on a high.

'The team is in a great place' - reaction

Bristol director of rugby Pat Lam told BBC Radio Bristol:

"We generally believed that we could win this game but, ultimately, we couldn't apply enough pressure.

"We did some great stuff on defence, turned ball over, put the ball up, but the lineout we lost all momentum - our game really thrives on building pressure on the other team and getting scoreboard pressure and we certainly had opportunities.

"We end up losing the game by six points, two tries were conceded with 13 men, that made it difficult.

"When you're playing a team like Leicester you need scoreboard pressure and line-out pressure and we couldn't do either. But that doesn't take away from the effort the boys put in."

Leicester head coach Geoff Parling told BBC Radio Leicester:

"Good, gritty win against a good team in a difficult place to come. Really proud of the guys, some frustrations at the end, spoke to Ches [Ollie Chessum] afterwards because I thought we could have iced it earlier which is a sign that the team is in a great place.

"Really proud of what we've done - we've had three games in 12 days again. Really proud of the team, 10 guys away at the start of the week, no excuses we just got on with it.

"I'm really pleased with what the group is putting out, not just on game day but also during the week and in training."

Replacements : Gwilliam, Woolmore, Chawatama, Caulfield, Owen, Marmion, Bates, Grondona.

articles.title: Bristol 16-22 Leicester: Tigers top Gallagher PREM table after beating Bears at Ashton Gate
articles.summary: Leicester beat Bristol 22-16 at Ashton Gate and move to the top of the Gallagher PREM table; Leicester scored 10 points when Bristol had two players sin-binned as they secured a bonus-point victory with tries from Freddie Steward, Adam Radwin, Ollie Hassell-Collins and Jamie Blamire
articles.body:
Tigers took advantage of Bristol having two men in the sin-bin to score 10 points in their absence, which ultimately proved the difference.

Leicester's tries came from Freddie Steward, Adam Radwin, Ollie Hassell-Collins and Jamie Blamire, with Billy Searle adding one conversion.

Louis Rees-Zammit scored the Bears' only try, with James Williams adding three penalties and a conversion to secure a losing bonus point.

Bristol took a sixth-minute lead thanks to a solo effort from the Welsh flyer Rees-Zammit. The wing received possession 35 metres out from the try-line, but from an unpromising position, he skipped past two defenders to race in under the posts.

Leicester's response was swift with bursts from Finn Carduff and Cameron Henderson putting the defence on the back foot before a well-judged cross-field kick from Searle saw Steward collect to crash over.

Minutes later, the visitors looked to have taken the lead when their skipper Ollie Chessum forced his way over, but TMO replays showed the ball had gone forward when Aaron Wainwright's penetrative run was brought to an end.

Bristol also came close when Rees-Zammit was presented with another opportunity but under pressure from the challenge of Tom Whiteley, he just failed to collect his own kick ahead as the line beckoned.

The hosts then suffered two blows in quick succession when centre Mathias Moroni and full-back Tom Jordan were both yellow carded for dangerous challenges.

Leicester capitalised when an alert Searle sent a long kick deep into the opposition 22 with Radwan showing exceptional speed to be first to the ball and touch down.

Radwan almost had another when he chased another kick ahead, but this time he failed to gather so the Tigers had to be content with a 12-7 interval lead.

Ninety seconds after the restart, Leicester extended their advantage when another cross-field kick found Hassell-Collins in acres of space to score his side's third.

Bristol were brought back to full strength before Williams reduced the arrears with a straightforward penalty.

Basic handling errors from Radwan and replacement Will Wand gave the Bears the chance to build an attacking platform, but they were too frenetic to benefit until Williams knocked over a second penalty.

The game hung in the balance but the away pack produced an unstoppable line-out drive for Blamire to secure the bonus point, with Searle missing his third conversion to keep the home side in the hunt.

A third penalty from Williams, seven minutes from time, set up a tense finish, but the Tigers held on for a deserved victory despite Searle hitting a post with a last-minute penalty.

articles.title: United States 12-55 England: Red Roses return to winning ways
articles.summary: England's Red Roses return to winning ways, but without entirely vanquishing doubts over their position at the top of the women's game, as they see off the United States.
articles.body:
Tries: Moloney-MacDonald (4), Jones, Venner, Field, Feaunati, Kabeya Cons: Sing (2), Harrison (3)

England's Red Roses returned to winning ways, but without entirely vanquishing doubts over their position at the top of the women's game, as they saw off a spirited United States in New Jersey.

England started steadily enough with wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald crossing twice in the first 12 minutes, her second coming via a looping mis-pass from fly-half Holly Aitchison.

However the United States, who were obliterated 69-7 in the opening match of England's march to the Rugby World Cup last year, stuck in the contest far longer than they did that day in Sunderland.

The sixth-ranked underdogs were still snarling deep into the second half with one thunderous hit from Alev Kelter, hoisting and dumping England captain Meg Jones, rallying her team.

Ultimately Moloney-MacDonald ran in four tries as England exploited space out wide, but their final performance of the WXV Global Series, after two losses to Canada over the previous fortnight, will give head coach John Mitchell plenty to ponder before the start of their Women's Six Nations title defence in April.

The United States claimed a second try with the final play of the match as Kate Zackary dived over around the fringes at the end of a surge that summed up their determination.

Watch all nine tries as England return to winning ways against USA

While Mitchell will undoubtedly take positives – Holly Aitchison's play-making and Maud Muir's all-action performance among them – he has plenty on his to-do list.

Top will be to tune up his team's set-piece solidity and attacking fluency.

England suffered at the line-out early on, unable to fire up their rolling maul from two promising attacking positions before being shoved back over their own line, only for Kathryn Treder's try to be ruled out for a obstruction call.

Muir was pinged as the experienced Hope Rogers grappled for set-piece supremacy.

And, all the while, the hosts were making headway at the gainline, buying territory with brute physicality - an aspect of the game which is usually England's trademark.

The United States got their reward as Rogers burrowed beneath Maddie Feaunati for a short-range score that sparked lasting celebrations.

Jones went over after full-back Emma Sing hit a good line to restore a 10-point lead by the break, but the stats below the scoreboard favoured the United States with the hosts enjoying more territory and possession and making more metres with the ball in hand at the interval.

Moloney-MacDonald's third and fourth scores soon after the restart put England 20 points clear and the outcome out of doubt.

The United States, who came into the match on the back of five-match winning run that includes successes over Ireland and South Africa, hung tough however.

While England's endurance and depth told, with Hannah Botterman impressing off the bench, Ellie Kildunne weaving up from backfield on her introduction and four tries scored in the final quarter, the hosts' energy was impressive.

Even with replacement prop Mona Lisa Tupou being sent to the sin bin for a scrum infringement, their resistance and physicality stayed high and was rewarded with Zackary's late score.

With both the attendance and the playing surface appearing patchy at the 25,000-capacity Sports Illustrated Stadium, organisers will hope to have a more impressive platform in place by the time the Women's Rugby World Cup is held stateside in 2033.

articles.title: USA 12-55 England: Red Roses return to winning ways as Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scores four tries in WXV Global Series
articles.summary: England's Red Roses score nine tries through Claudia Moloney-MacDonald (four), Meg Jones, Mia Venner, Bryony Field, Maddie Feaunati, Sadia Kabeya in WXV Global Series thrashing of USA in New Jersey; win sees Red Roses respond following shock back-to-back losses in Canada
articles.body:
John Mitchell's side entered the contest off the back of losing two Tests in a row for the first time in a decade, and having lost their 41-Test, four-year unbeaten run in Toronto.

A competitive first half against the USA saw 10 points in it at half-time, but the second half proved largely one-way traffic as England's superiority showed.

In all, the Red Roses scored nine tries through wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald (four), centre Meg Jones, wing Mia Venner, replacement hooker Bryony Field and back-rows Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya.

The USA scored two tries through loosehead prop Hope Rogers and replacement back Kate Zackary, but shipped three second-half tries in nine minutes with prop Mona Tupou in the sin-bin due to repeat scrum penalties.

Jones: We'll review this tour - we're hungry to get better

Red Roses captain Meg Jones said post-match:

"First of all, credit to the USA, I think they've come off the back of some amazing wins and gained so much momentum. They are doing such a good effort there, building and growing the game.

"For us, we just wanted to control the game and impose ourselves on them.

"When we got into it, we kept the ball and everyone was a threat at the line. That's when we were unstoppable.

"Off the back of two losses, we just wanted to learn, and we'll continue to learn. We've got so much feedback from this tour.

"We'll go and review it, reflect, and see where we can keep growing. Because I know there is so much growth in this team.

Moloney-MacDonald: Tonight was about proving it to ourselves

Player-of-the-match Moloney-MacDonald said:

"This week was all about proving it to ourselves.

"We've obviously had three really tough games against Canada, and the last two weeks did not go the way we wanted it to go.

"For us, it was about learning as much as we possibly could from those two performances. A challenge we've never really been faced with previously.

"We spoke a lot about going out there and being fearless tonight. That's exactly what we did. We attacked it from minute zero to minute 80.

"I'm just so proud of the girls, the way we turned up today.

"That's what the Red Roses is all about."

Perris-Redding: We were in the game in first half - result does not take away our growth

USA co-captain Georgie Perris-Redding said:

"We were in it in the first half, and that was really tough because I was so proud of the girls.

"We came into this game confident, you've seen the streak we've had and we've been building.

"We lost it a bit in the second half, so it's frustrating.

"But I am so proud of the growth this team has made. Today's result does not take that away."
